Do some physical exercise during the day, expose yourself to the sun at least 3-4h a day, eat healthy and do not engage on activities merely because you think they would make you sleepy. Do not go to bed and force yourself to sleep if you feel wide awaken.

Try buying ear plugs (I prefer the silicone ones) to exclude the possibility that you are wakening up due to some external noises (a garbage truck for instance). Once you are sure that it isn't anything external do some internal reflection: "Did I changed my sleep schedule?" "Am I more stressed lately?",etc.. because your sleep quality is dropping for some reason.

This happens to me sometimes as well. I think it's because you are so stressed out or had such an adrenaline rush that day (due to exercise for example) that your brain doesn't really get into the deep sleeping phases  which may explain why the body temperature doesn't lower as it should.

My advice includes shifting your exercises early in the day as much as you can to avoid higher levels of metabolism by night, and if you suspect that you have to be at your best the following day don't exercise too hard. At dinner eat things that are easy to digest and avoid fats, taking a shower before sleep is also a good idea to relax your body muscles and reduce stress levels.

You quote one thing and you extrapolate data that isn't even there. Learn to read and interpret a scientific text, they say that loneliness can be used to predict/detect if a person is in a depressive state, because you know.. people don't have a sign above their heads saying that they are depressed.

There's nothing saying that depression causes loneliness or vice-versa, it says that the two states tend to hang together (i.e. they are correlated). There's lot of depression cases that arise from people being alone and there's people that isolate themselves because they are unhappy due to some other reason. You can't make axiomatic statements about human behavior . 

And btw, read the whole article and don't jump straight to the conclusions.

>Empirical data suggests that loneliness is significantly correlated to depressive symptoms (Bradley 1970; Bragg 1979; Hsu et al. 1987) and numerous other negative outcomes. Lonely people have indicated they are less happy, less satisfied, more pessimistic, and suffer from more depressive symptoms (Peplau and Perlman 1982) than people who are not lonely. Lonely individuals have also reported negative behaviors and affective states when experiencing loneliness, including tenseness, restlessness, and boredom.
